gold.abstract: Participation incentives is a well-known issue inhibiting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in medicine, as well as a potential cause of user dissatisfaction for RCTs in online platforms. We frame this issue as a non-standard exploration-exploitation tradeoff: an RCT would like to explore as uniformly as possible, whereas each "agent" (a patient or a user) prefers "exploitation", i.e., treatments that seem best. We incentivize participation by leveraging information asymmetry between the trial and the agents. We measure statistical performance via worst-case estimation error under adversarially generated outcomes, a standard objective for RCTs. We obtain a near-optimal solution in terms of this objective: an incentive-compatible mechanism with a particular guarantee, and a nearly matching impossibility result for any incentive-compatible mechanism. We consider three model variants: homogeneous agents (of the same "type" comprising beliefs and preferences), heterogeneous agents, and an extension that leverages estimated type frequencies to mitigate the influence of rare-but-difficult agent types.

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b contributes a taxonomy of adaptive clinical trial designs—prospective, concurrent (ad hoc), retrospective—and warns that adaptations may shift the actual patient population and inflate type I error; it also identifies implementation barriers and rare-disease strategies.
Paper-c contributes a conjoint-analysis method showing Alzheimer’s disease study partners value home visits (utility 0.89), which offsets high intervention risk disutility (-0.85); car service is redundant; inconvenience reduction correlates with disease severity and may increase participation.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use paper-c’s preference-measurement method to quantify willingness to participate under adaptation features described by paper-b. Operationally, “adaptation type” becomes a trial-design attribute in a conjoint experiment: fixed, prospective adaptive, or ad hoc amendment. Paper-b supplies the risk/validity features of these adaptations; paper-c supplies the mechanism linking design attributes and amenities to enrollment utility. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing data jointly measure adaptive-design features and participant preferences.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Recruit AD study partners and present hypothetical trial scenarios varying five attributes: adaptation type (fixed vs prospective vs ad hoc), home visits (yes/no), car service (yes/no), chance of receiving active intervention, and disclosed risk of altered trial validity/type I error. Measure willingness to allow participation. Hypotheses: prospective adaptation will have smaller disutility than ad hoc amendment; home visits will offset adaptation-related disutility. Estimate mixed logit utilities and predicted enrollment shares. Validate by comparing predicted participation with actual recruitment in a subsequent pilot AD trial using the highest-utility design.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether prospective adaptive trial features can be redesigned to maintain AD study partner willingness by combining adaptive-design risk taxonomy with conjoint preference measurement. It quantifies how adaptation type, home visits, and intervention chance jointly predict enrollment. If home visits offset adaptation disutility, trialists could use preference-based redesign to reduce recruitment delays while monitoring adaptation-related validity risks.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating adaptive-design risk features from clinical trial methodology with conjoint preference measurement can predict and offset enrollment losses caused by trial adaptations in Alzheimer’s disease studies.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper B reviews adaptive clinical trial designs, classifying them as prospective, concurrent, or retrospective, and warns that unplanned adaptations may shift the patient population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper C uses conjoint analysis in 108 AD study partners: home visits had the highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service was redundant; low-risk/high-active-treatment predicted 60% willingness; reduced travel hassle correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use Paper C’s measured utility weights as pre-specified adaptation thresholds inside Paper B’s prospective adaptive design. At interim, if enrollment/retention falls below a boundary or caregiver burden exceeds a utility-weighted threshold, the trial adds home visits for future participants. This connects preference measurement operationally to adaptive trial rules, not merely shared topic.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Simulation plus pilot two-stage AD trial. Primary outcome: ADAS-Cog change; measure caregiver burden, AD severity, travel burden, and baseline conjoint utilities. Pre-specify adaptation: at n=50, if observed retention <70% and home-visit utility ≥0.89, switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. Compare type I error, power, recruitment time, and retention against a fixed design. Validate by re-estimating conjoint utilities in the enrolled sample and comparing predicted vs actual willingness. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source has joint data on adaptive logistics and AD outcomes; this study would generate it.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Adaptive trials risk population drift, while AD trials struggle with recruitment and retention. This project embeds conjoint-derived participant preferences into a prospective adaptive design, using home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim trigger. Simulations and a pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived utilities for home visits as pre-specified adaptation triggers in prospective adaptive clinical trials to improve recruitment/retention while controlling type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper B reviews adaptive clinical trial designs, classifying them as prospective, concurrent, or retrospective, and warns that unplanned adaptations may shift the patient population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper C uses conjoint analysis in 108 AD study partners: home visits had the highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service was redundant; low-risk/high-active-treatment predicted 60% willingness; reduced travel hassle correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use Paper C’s measured utility weights as pre-specified adaptation thresholds inside Paper B’s prospective adaptive design. At interim, if enrollment/retention falls below a boundary or caregiver burden exceeds a utility-weighted threshold, the trial adds home visits for future participants. This connects preference measurement operationally to adaptive trial rules, not merely shared topic.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Simulation plus pilot two-stage AD trial. Primary outcome: ADAS-Cog change; measure caregiver burden, AD severity, travel burden, and baseline conjoint utilities. Pre-specify adaptation: at n=50, if observed retention <70% and home-visit utility ≥0.89, switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. Compare type I error, power, recruitment time, and retention against a fixed design. Validate by re-estimating conjoint utilities in the enrolled sample and comparing predicted vs actual willingness. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source has joint data on adaptive logistics and AD outcomes; this study would generate it.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Adaptive trials risk population drift, while AD trials struggle with recruitment and retention. This project embeds conjoint-derived participant preferences into a prospective adaptive design, using home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim trigger. Simulations and a pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived utilities for home visits as pre-specified adaptation triggers in prospective adaptive clinical trials to improve recruitment/retention while controlling type I error.
